column11: Category\n"What is the main role of an Operating System?"
column20: An Operating System acts as an intermediary between user applications and computer hardware, managing CPU, memory, storage, and I/O devices.
column21: OS Basics - General Concepts\n"Which of the following is an example of a desktop operating system?"
column30: Microsoft Windows is a widely used desktop/laptop OS, whereas Android and iOS are mobile operating systems.
column31: OS Basics - General Concepts\n"Which operating system is developed by Apple for iPhones?"
column40: iOS is Apple's proprietary mobile operating system created exclusively for its iPhone hardware.
column41: OS Basics - General Concepts\n"Which OS function organizes and retrieves files?"
column50: File Management manages files and directories on storage drives, providing structured access, naming, and retrieval.
column51: OS Basics - General Concepts\n"Which operating system is open-source and highly customizable?"
column60: Linux is released under open-source licenses (GPL), allowing users and developers to inspect, modify, and distribute its source code.
column61: OS Basics - General Concepts\n"What is a process?"
column70: A process is defined as an active program in execution loaded into memory with its program counter, stack, and data.
column71: OS Basics - General Concepts\n"Which process management function decides the next process to use the CPU?"
column80: CPU Scheduling determines which process in the ready queue is allocated CPU time.
column81: OS Basics - General Concepts\n"Which memory management technique uses disk space as extra memory?"
column90: Virtual Memory maps secondary disk storage into virtual address space, enabling execution of processes larger than physical RAM.
column91: OS Basics - General Concepts\n"Which file operation removes a file?"
column100: The Delete operation unlinks and frees the file blocks in the file system.
column101: OS Basics - General Concepts\n"What acts as an interface between hardware and the OS?"
column110: A Device Driver is specialized software that provides a standardized interface for the OS to communicate with physical hardware.
column111: OS Basics - General Concepts\n"Which technique manages print jobs in a queue?"
column120: SPOOLing (Simultaneous Peripheral Operations On-Line) buffers print data to disk until the printer is ready to process it.
column121: OS Basics - General Concepts\n"Which OS processes jobs in groups without user interaction?"
column130: A Batch Operating System groups similar jobs together in batches and executes them sequentially without interactive user intervention.
column131: OS Structures & Types\n"Which OS allows multiple CPUs to execute processes simultaneously?"
column140: A Multiprocessing OS coordinates two or more CPUs to run independent process threads in parallel.
column141: OS Structures & Types\n"Which OS manages a group of networked computers as a single system?"
column150: A Distributed OS connects autonomous computing nodes across a network, presenting them as a unified single computer system.
column160: RTOS stands for Real-Time Operating System, designed to guarantee response within strict latency and timing deadlines.
column161: OS Structures & Types\n"Which OS structure has no well-defined architecture?"
column170: A Simple Structure (like original MS-DOS) lacks clean separation between interfaces and levels of functionality.
column171: OS Structures & Types\n"Which operating system is an example of a simple structure?"
column180: MS-DOS was designed with a simple structure where applications could access basic I/O routines and hardware directly.
column181: OS Structures & Types\n"Which structure divides the OS into multiple layers?"
column190: A Layered OS is decomposed into hierarchical layers where Layer N uses only services provided by Layer N-1.
column191: OS Structures & Types\n"Which OS structure uses dynamically loadable modules?"
column200: Modular Structure allows kernel extensions and drivers to be loaded and linked dynamically at runtime.
column201: OS Structures & Types\n"VirtualBox is an example of:"
column210: VirtualBox is a hypervisor/virtualization platform that provides Virtual Machine environments.
column211: OS Structures & Types\n"Which structure contains all services in one large kernel?"
column220: A Monolithic kernel combines all OS services (scheduling, memory, file system, IPC, device drivers) into a single address space.
column221: OS Structures & Types\n"Which OS structure runs non-essential services in user space?"
column230: A Microkernel keeps only fundamental mechanisms (IPC, basic scheduling, memory mapping) in kernel mode and moves servers to user space.
column231: OS Structures & Types\n"Which OS structure allows services to be dynamically added to the kernel at runtime?"
column240: Modular kernel architectures (like Linux Loadable Kernel Modules - LKMs) permit dynamic loading/unloading without rebooting.
column241: OS Structures & Types\n"Which OS structure organizes components into layers where each layer uses services of the lower layer?"
column250: In a Layered architecture, the lowest layer (Layer 0) is hardware and the highest is user interface, with each layer communicating strictly with adjacent lower layers.
column251: OS Structures & Types\n"In which era was UNIX introduced?"
column260: UNIX was originally developed between 1969 and the 1970s by Ken Thompson, Dennis Ritchie, and others at AT&T Bell Labs.
column261: UNIX & Linux Specifics\n"Which security mechanism verifies users through credentials?"
column270: Authentication is the process of confirming user identity using credentials such as usernames, passwords, or cryptographic keys.
column280: Linus Torvalds created the Linux kernel in 1991 while a student at the University of Helsinki.
column281: UNIX & Linux Specifics\n"UNIX was originally developed at:"
column290: UNIX was pioneered at AT&T Bell Labs in Murray Hill, New Jersey.
column291: UNIX & Linux Specifics\n"Which UNIX component acts as the interface between user and kernel?"
column300: The Shell (e.g. bash, sh, zsh) is the command-line command interpreter that accepts user commands and executes corresponding system requests.
column301: UNIX & Linux Specifics\n"Which is a key feature of UNIX?"
column310: UNIX was fundamentally designed from its early versions to support multiple simultaneous users (Multi-user) and preemptive multitasking.
column311: UNIX & Linux Specifics\n"Which Linux layer contains device drivers?"
column320: In monolithic Linux architecture, hardware device drivers execute inside Kernel Space with direct hardware privileged access.
column321: UNIX & Linux Specifics\n"Linux is licensed as:"
column330: Linux is licensed under the GNU General Public License (GPL), making it Open Source.
column331: UNIX & Linux Specifics\n"A company wants a free
column335: with strong community support and frequent updates. Which OS is most suitable?"
column344: Linux distributions (Ubuntu Server, Debian, RHEL, Rocky) dominate server, cloud, and container infrastructures due to open licensing and massive global support.
column345: UNIX & Linux Specifics\n"What is the main purpose of a system call?"
column347: Provide an interface between user programs and the operating system
column354: System calls provide the programmatic interface between a running application and kernel-level services.
column355: System Calls & Modes\n"System calls act as a gateway between:"
column364: System calls trigger a software trap or sysenter instruction that transitions execution from unprivileged User mode to privileged Kernel mode.
column365: System Calls & Modes\n"Which mode executes system calls?"
column374: The kernel executes the privileged system call handler instructions in Kernel mode (Ring 0).
column375: System Calls & Modes\n"Which system call is commonly used to display output on the screen in POSIX/UNIX?"
column384: The write() system call writes bytes from a buffer to a file descriptor (such as stdout / fd 1).
column385: System Calls & Modes\n"Which of the following is NOT a type of system call?"
column394: Compilers are user-space software tools; Operating Systems provide system calls for Process Control, File, Device, Info, and Communications, but not Compiler Management.
column404: A program is a passive entity stored on disk (executable file), whereas a process is an active entity in execution.
column405: Process & Thread Management\n"Which section of a process contains executable code?"
column414: The Text segment (or code segment) stores the compiled binary machine code instructions.
column415: Process & Thread Management\n"Which section stores global variables in a process?"
column424: The Data segment holds initialized and uninitialized global and static variables.
column426: malloc in C) occurs in the:"
column435: The Heap is the memory region dynamically allocated at runtime via malloc/new and deallocated with free/delete.
column436: Process & Thread Management\n"Function parameters and local variables are stored in the:"
column445: The Stack allocates activation records containing function parameters, return addresses, and local stack variables.
column446: Process & Thread Management\n"Which process state indicates that instructions are currently being executed?"
column455: In the Running state, CPU instructions for the process are actively being executed on a processor core.
column456: Process & Thread Management\n"A process waiting to be assigned to the CPU is in the:"
column465: The Ready state contains processes in memory that are ready to run as soon as CPU time is scheduled.
column466: Process & Thread Management\n"Which process state indicates the process has finished execution?"
column475: The Terminated (or Exit) state indicates that the process has finished execution and its OS resources are being cleaned up.
column485: Process Control Block (PCB) is the primary kernel data structure storing all state and accounting details for a process.
column486: Process & Thread Management\n"Which PCB field stores the address of the next instruction?"
column495: The Program Counter (PC) register contains the memory address of the next instruction to be fetched and executed.
column496: Process & Thread Management\n"Context switching occurs when:"
column498: CPU switches from one process to another
column505: Context switching saves the current process state into its PCB and restores another process's state to switch execution.
column506: Process & Thread Management\n"During a context switch
column507: the process context is saved in the:"
column516: The CPU registers, PC, stack pointer, and state are preserved in the Process Control Block (PCB).
column519: A basic unit of CPU utilization
column526: A thread is a lightweight execution flow inside a process and represents the basic unit of CPU scheduling.
column527: Process & Thread Management\n"Threads of the same process share:"
column536: Threads in a shared process share the code section, data section, heap, and open file descriptors, while having independent stacks and registers.
column537: Process & Thread Management\n"Which threading model maps many user threads to one kernel thread?"
column546: The Many-to-One model maps multiple user-space threads to a single kernel thread, but a blocking system call blocks all user threads.
column547: Process & Thread Management\n"Which threading model is used by Linux (NPTL)?"
column556: Linux Native POSIX Thread Library (NPTL) utilizes the One-to-One threading model where each user thread maps to a kernel schedulable entity (task_struct).
column557: Process & Thread Management\n"Which threading model maps many user threads to many kernel threads?"
column566: The Many-to-Many model multiplexes many user threads onto a smaller or equal number of kernel threads.
column567: Process & Thread Management\n"Which of the following is a CPU scheduling criterion?"
column576: CPU Scheduling criteria include CPU Utilization, Throughput, Turnaround Time, Waiting Time, and Response Time.
column578: Number of completed processes per unit time
column586: Throughput is the count of processes that complete their execution per unit of time (e.g. processes per minute).
column587: CPU Scheduling\n"Which scheduling method allows a running process to be interrupted?"
column596: Preemptive scheduling allows the OS scheduler to interrupt and suspend an actively executing process to allocate the CPU to another process.
column598: the CPU is released when the process:"
column607: In non-preemptive scheduling, once the CPU has been allocated to a process, the process keeps the CPU until it releases it either by terminating or by switching to the waiting state.
column617: FCFS stands for First Come First Serve scheduling.
column618: CPU Scheduling\n"FCFS scheduling follows which queue discipline?"
column627: FCFS scheduling operates on a First-In, First-Out (FIFO) queue discipline.
column647: SJF stands for Shortest Job First scheduling.
column648: CPU Scheduling\n"SJF scheduling selects the process with the:"
column657: SJF associates each process with its next CPU burst length and schedules the process with the shortest CPU burst first.
column658: CPU Scheduling\n"The preemptive version of SJF is known as:"
column667: SRTF (Shortest Remaining Time First) is the preemptive implementation of Shortest Job First scheduling.
column668: CPU Scheduling\n"Round Robin scheduling uses a fixed:"
column677: Round Robin (RR) allocates a fixed time slice called a Time Quantum (or time slice) to each process in circular order.
column678: CPU Scheduling\n"Round Robin scheduling is a:"
column687: Round Robin is inherently preemptive because when the time quantum expires, a timer interrupt forces a context switch.
column688: CPU Scheduling\n"A Gantt chart is used to:"
column697: A Gantt chart is a horizontal bar chart that visually illustrates the timeline and process schedule execution across the CPU.
